title.en: The Elephant That Stole the Mantis's Springbok

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1874 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the Elephants'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §12

summary.en: Digging honey, the Mantis throws it up to his pet springbok; the elephant substitutes her calf, who answers 'Kurru!' The Mantis kills the impostor, tracks the herd, enters the mother at the navel, cuts her whole inside to pieces and comes out at her trunk with the child on his back as she falls dead.
summary.zh: 螳螂掘蜜擲予寵羚；母象以己子代之，答曰「庫魯！」。螳螂殺其偽者，追象群，自其臍入，碎其內臟，自其鼻而出，背負幼羚——母象倒斃。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Elephant carried off the little Springbok, while the Mantis was digging in the hole... The Mantis was digging out wild bees' honey and throwing it to the little Springbok. He said: 'Are you eating, as I am eating?'... Then the Elephant calf said: 'Kurru!' And the Mantis said: 'Listen! What is the matter? My child does not usually speak so that I cannot understand it.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 41 (public domain).

passages.text: Then the Mantis got out of the hole; he found the Elephant calf sitting covered up with earth, he said: 'It must have been this person.'... This person must have been sitting here, his ears look like a mat lying there... And he killed the Elephant calf... He caught sight of the spoor of a troop of Elephants.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 41, 43 (public domain).

passages.text: Then the Elephants caught sight of him as he came over the hill, and the Mother Elephant arose and rushed out. She picked up the little Springbok and swallowed it... The Mantis said: 'I will get into your mouth.' And the Elephant replied that she would spit him out. Then the Mantis said he would get in under her fingernail... but he got into her navel, and the other Elephants stabbed at him with their spears as he went in.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 43-44 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: The Mantis cut the Elephant's whole inside to pieces, and while the Elephants were watching for him at the other Elephant's navel... he came out at the Elephant's trunk, came out above her head carrying the little Springbok on his back, while the Elephant fell down dead... he spoke as he flew away: 'Can you equal me? I am the Mantis... he is an enchanter, from whom you tried to steal his child.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 44 (public domain).

title.en: The Kwai-kwai Bird, the Mantis and the Children

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Kwai-kwai Bird, the Mantis and the Children'

summary.en: The Kwai-kwai, once a man, nets the children to kill them; the Mantis, dreaming it, stays home as their grown-up guard. When the bird comes, he has the children roast the Kwai-kwai on hot stones — 'for it is merely a Kwai-kwai' — and it screams 'I ought always to look where the Mantis is.'
summary.zh: 怪鴟本為人，網羅孩童欲殺之；螳螂夢而知之，留家守護。鴟至，螳螂令孩童以熱石炙之——「不過一怪鴟耳」。鴟號曰：「吾當常察螳螂何在。」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; contains implied child-killing theme in a warning-fable frame; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Kwai-kwai bird was once a man. He put children into a net. Then the children sang about him... 'Mother, mother, The Kwai-kwai Is taking us to kill, Tho' we stayed at home!' Then Grandfather Mantis said: 'Call loudly, call, call loudly!'... Their mothers said: 'You must listen, our little ones are calling out!... The children speak with a small voice, while Grandfather speaks with a deep voice. Therefore I think he is walking, he is listening for us.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 45 (public domain).

passages.text: The Mantis felt that he had been dreaming, that the Kwai-kwai had come in anger to the children... Therefore he, the Mantis, he who was wise would stay with the children at home, for children are ignorant... Then he spoke to the children, he said: 'Children, roast the Kwai-kwai, for it is merely a Kwai-kwai.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 45-46 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: Then the children roasted the Kwai-kwai on hot stones, that is how they roasted him. And the Kwai-kwai screamed because of the burns... And the Kwai-kwai said: 'Vvvvvvv, I ought always to look where the Mantis is.' The Mantis said: 'I am the Mantis, I am here!... I am the one who is roasting you; I am the one who is clever!'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 46 (public domain).

title.en: The Dasse's Story and the Crow's Story

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Dasse's Story and the Crow's Story'

summary.en: The Mantis's pranks bring falling stones down on Kwammang-a, who is hidden in a gambro hollow; the ring-necked crows sent out eat their neck-fat halfway home. The pied Crow flies on, and Kwammang-a's face and body are dug out — but Kauru must beg before they will take out her trickster husband, whom they drag roughly from the stones.
summary.zh: 螳螂戲耍致落石壓誇曼加，其藏於瓜布羅果洞中；環頸鴉半途食盡頸脂而返。白頸鴉飛達，誇曼加面體得掘出——唯卡烏魯哀求，眾方拔其夫，粗暴拖出。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Kwammang-a once went visiting. They were two, he and the Mantis, and they went to the Bees' house... Then a young Bee offered Kwammang-a his ostrich egg-shell... while a young Dasse offered the Mantis his ostrich egg-shell, into which he had put dirty water... When he tasted the Dasse's dirty water, he cursed the young Dasse.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 47 (public domain).

passages.text: Then the Mother Dasse, who was on the hunting-ground, sneezed, and drops of blood came from her nostrils. Therefore stones rolled... Then the young Bee spoke to his Grandfather Kwammang-a... 'You get into it, for the Mantis was really with you, that man who has been teasing. Therefore hard things are falling upon you.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 47 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: The people said: 'What can be the matter? You ought to send the ring-necked Crow, that it may go and see where the people are.' And the ring-necked Crow went; it had on its neck a little piece of fat which was very small. It went and ate up the fat half-way and it turned back. And the little piece of fat is that which sits white on its neck.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 47-48 (public domain).

passages.text: The Elephant and the Giraffe and the Rhinoceros were those who went to take out Kwammang-a's party... Then, when she saw that the people meant to leave the Mantis, she told the people to take the Mantis out for her, because he was her husband... Then the people took hold and uncovered the stones, and the people pulled the Mantis out roughly, hurting him.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 48-49 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Korotwiten: Why the Ground Must Be Shared
title.zh: 科羅蒂滕：大地必須分享

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis and the Korotwiten'

summary.en: The Korotwiten, once a man, hovers and dives into ant-holes, carrying out a full kaross of Bushman-rice at another hole. The Mantis imitates him, breaks his bow, quiver and digging-stick, and scoops rice without sharing; the angry bird makes the ground hard, and the Mantis, plunging to enter an ant-hole, crashes on his brow bleeding. Share with the Korotwiten, Kwammang-a says, and the ground opens.
summary.zh: 科羅蒂滕本為人，翔而入蟻穴，自他穴拖出滿皮衣之蟻卵。螳螂仿之，折弓毀囊棄掘杖，取米而不分；鳥怒，令地變硬；螳螂撲穴，撞額流血。夸曼加曰：與科羅蒂滕分享，地自開。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San myth from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Korotwiten is a little bird; it is black; it has white feathers on its shoulders. It was once a man; it was one of the Early Race... The Korotwiten dropped down, he dived into a little ant-hole, while the Mantis stood looking at him. And lo! he carried out the kaross from another little ant-hole... a kaross full of 'Bushman rice'.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 50 (public domain).

passages.text: The Mantis said: 'You must please anoint me, for you can do this, but I have to dig Bushman rice out with a stick. Therefore my hands are sore...' Then the Korotwiten spoke... 'You should go up to an ant heap... you should watch.' And the Mantis said: 'You can give me (the power) to see.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 50-51 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: Then the Mantis broke the bow across his foot, he snapped the arrow in two, he tore up the quiver, he also struck and split the digging stone, he struck and broke the digging stick... Then he hovered and hovered in the air, he dived into a little ant-hole, and he verily carried out a karossful of Bushman rice at another place.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 51 (public domain).

passages.text: And the Mantis woke up early... he went to hover above it. And he kept hovering there, he dropped down, he tried to dive in, he plunged on to his brow. And he cried with the pain in his brow... he again hovered above, he dropped down, he again crashed on to the front of his head, while blood flowed... 'Father wishes me to say, he told you to share with the Korotwiten, for the earth would be hard for us, if the Korotwiten were angry.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 53-54 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: Ku-te-gaua and the Mantis: Cats Out of the Fire
title.zh: 庫特加瓦與螳螂：火中之貓

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'Ku-te-gaua and the Mantis'

summary.en: Ku-te-gaua sets wildcat lairs ablaze and steps into the fire unburnt, dragging out peerless cats, singing 'Ku-te-gaua, n bagen, bagen, gaua!' The Mantis imitates him and the fire feels cool — until he refuses Ku-te-gaua a share. Then the cats burn up and the fire scorches the Mantis: the fire is quiet only for those who give every other cat.
summary.zh: 庫特加瓦縱火焚野貓穴，裸步入火不傷，拖出無雙之貓，唱「庫特加瓦，恩巴根，巴根，加瓦！」。螳螂仿之，火覺清涼——直至拒予其一。貓盡焚，火灼螳螂：唯肯隔一予一者，火乃靜。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San myth from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Ku-te-gaua used once to set fire to the lairs of wildcats. Then he got into the fire and brought out the wild cats, and those cats had no equals in beauty... he would set fire to the lair, he would get into the fire, when the fire was burning, yet the fire would feel cool and not feel hot, because it felt that he was the one who owned the fire.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 54 (public domain).

passages.text: Then the Mantis took a firebrand, he went up to a lair. He set fire to the lair, he sang again... for he imitated Ku-te-gaua... And he jumped into the fire, he dragged out cats, he laid them down... because he was glad that the fire did not burn him.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 55 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: Then Ku-te-gaua exclaimed: 'O Man! You shall give me a share of these cats, or else you will find out what the fire feels like; because you act like this, while we are wont to give to one another.'... 'Wait, you shall feel the fire to-morrow... those cats shall be burnt up, the fire shall burn you badly, when you try to enter the fire.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 56-57 (public domain).

passages.text: Then the Mantis set out, he reached a lair, he set fire to the lair, he sang again... Then he sprang into the fire, and he was scorched in the fire. He exclaimed: 'Hartebeest's children, you must go!' and he flew down, he popped into the water... Then Kwammang-a spoke... 'we are wont to do so, when we want the fire to be quiet and feel cool for us... For we are wont to give him every other cat.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 57-58 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: Why the Wildebeest Has a Light Tail

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'Why the Wildebeest has a light Tail'

summary.en: The black wildebeest unties the Longnosed Mice's bowstrings, strings his own entrails on them, blunts their arrows, then tramples their hiding-screens as the quaggas stream past. The Mantis dreams the murders; the Striped Mouse mounts new strings and hidden arrowheads, builds an invisible screen, and shoots the wildebeest through the armpits as he gallops up.
summary.zh: 黑角馬解長鼻鼠之弓弦，以己腸代之，鈍其箭鏃，俟斑馬群奔時踏碎其隱屏。螳螂夢知其殺戮；條紋鼠換新弦、備隱箭、築不見之屏，於其飛馳時射穿其腋。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Black Wildebeest used once to do as follows: when the Longnosed Mice were sticking up ostrich-feather brushes on the hunting-ground to drive the Quaggas, he came up to a Mouse as it sat watching, he untied the Mouse's bowstring and swallowed it, and he strung on his own entrails for the Mouse; he blunted the Mouse's arrowheads.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 58 (public domain).

passages.text: And he arose, he went to take a piece of (a certain) grass, he made a tail for himself of this grass... Whenever he wanted to kill a man... he turned himself into a Quagga (by means of this tail which was like theirs)... He ran up to it, he went and stamped on it, crushing the Mouse, as he trod it down.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 58-59 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: The Striped Mouse took out a new bowstring, he untied and took off the entrails, he strung on the new bowstring. He took out arrowheads which were in the bag, he mounted them. He made a screen of bushes which was not small... He made a little screen of bushes which was not visible, which the Wildebeest did not see.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 59 (public domain).

passages.text: The Wildebeest ran on in front, he came looking as he ran, he saw the (larger) screen of bushes there. He ran up to it, and the Striped Mouse shot him right through the armpits. He snatched out the grass of which he had made himself a tail, he hurled it away, he went and lay down to die... The Striped Mouse made his people of the Longnosed Mice; he was strong, because he was clever. But the Mantis was the one who dreamt that that man had been killing the Longnosed Mice.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 59-60 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Lizard, the Mice and the Mantis

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Lizard, the Mice and the Mantis'

summary.en: The Kogelman lizard sings on the thorn-tree, calls each Longnosed Mouse in 'to take out the bag for daughter-in-law', makes him shut his eyes as he comes out, and knocks him down with a stick, then roasts springbok for his daughter. The Mantis dreams the murders; the Striped Mouse comes calling, refuses the rotten water-bag, refuses to dive, and is handed the stick by the Lizard's own daughter — 'dzap-p' — and the mice revive.
summary.zh: 蜥蜴歌於荊樹，呼長鼻鼠入洞「為媳取袋」，令其閉眼而出，以杖擊之；炙羚肉予其女。螳螂夢知其殺；條紋鼠至，拒臭水囊，拒入洞；蜥蜴之女親授其杖——「啪」——鼠輩復甦。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The 'Kogelman' Lizard once sat upon a 'Driedoorn' tree. He lay singing on the thorntree... 'Oh, oh! The Lizard lies on the thorntree.' And his daughter heard a Longnosed Mouse come calling; he called, as he followed a wounded springbok.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 60 (public domain).

passages.text: And he said: 'You must do like this, you must go in quickly, you must take out the bag for daughter-in-law.' And the Mouse went in. And he said: 'You must come turning your head back in this manner, as we do; you must shut your eyes, as you come out.'... The Mouse came out. He struck 'dzap-p', hitting the Mouse's face with the stick.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 60-61 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: The Striped Mouse said: 'If I go in, you will see that I cannot get in, for I shall stick fast, for the hole's mouth is not big enough for me to enter.'... The Lizard went in twisting about. The Girl went, she went to fetch the stick... She said: 'You will see your companions. This stick is the one with which he hit your companions.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 63-64 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: He shut his eyes coming out, and the Striped Mouse hit 'dzap-p', knocking him down at the hole's mouth. The Striped Mouse said: 'I am by myself killing to save my friends,' while the Longnosed Mice said: 'I am here, I am here!' and they lifted up their brushes, they waved their brushes.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 64 (public domain).

title.en: The Striped Mouse and the Beetle

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Striped Mouse and the Beetle'

summary.en: The Beetle, who was not strong but killed the Longnosed Mice for sport, throws his big stick 'habbu, pu, pu, pu'; the Striped Mouse throws back 'xet, te te te', knocks him down, and the dead mice come to life again, crying 'I am here!'
summary.zh: 甲蟲非強而以殺長鼻鼠為樂；擲巨棒「哈布噗噗噗」；條紋鼠擲回「克斯特特特特」，擊之倒地；死者群鼠復生，呼「我在此！我在此！」

sensitivity.note: |Xam San fable from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Longnosed Mice used to be people; they were not strong. Therefore the Beetle killed them. Then the Mantis dreamt about him... Then the wife of the Striped Mouse did this: when the Striped Mouse was a little way off, she sat up above there, sat sunning herself, because she was watching for her husband. Then she caught sight of the Beetle coming.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 65 (public domain).

passages.text: The Beetle said: 'Get out of the way, The Beetle is throwing.' And he threw 'habbu, pu, pu, pu, pu', hurling a stick, and the stick was not small. Then the Striped Mouse said: 'The Beetle is throwing, Get out of the way.' The Striped Mouse threw, 'xet, te te te te', letting fly back to the Beetle.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 65-66 (public domain).

passages.text: And the striped Mouse threw, 'xet te te te, te', knocking the Beetle down. Then the Striped Mouse said: 'I am by myself, killing to save my friends.' Then the Longnosed Mice came to life again, those whom the Beetle had killed. They came to life. They kept saying: 'I am here, I am here,' as they jumped up.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 66 (public domain).

title.en: The Colours in the Rainbow: Mantis Above, Kwammang-a Below
title.zh: 虹之色：上螳螂、下夸曼加

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Colours in the Rainbow'

summary.en: The rainbow is yellow above and red below, for the Mantis — who is also yellow — lies above and Kwammang-a below. Grown-ups call the rainbow Kwammang-a; and people say 'the Rainbow stands yonder and the rain will break.'
summary.zh: 虹上黃下赤：螳螂——其身亦黃——居上，夸曼加居下。長者稱虹為「夸曼加」；人曰「虹立於彼，雨將止」。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Rainbow is yellow in that part which lies above; the piece which seems red lies below. For the Mantis, who is also yellow, lies above, and Kwammang-a lies below. For the Mantis is the one whose part above is yellow, and that part which lies below is red, while that part which is above is yellow. It is the Rainbow. Men call it Kwammang-a. Therefore we who are children say 'Kwammang-a' to it, because the grown-up people said Kwammang-a to it... Then people say: 'The Rainbow stands yonder and the rain will break.'
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 66 (public domain).

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded c. 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Names of Places'

summary.en: It was the Mantis who once called the places names: |hii/hoa is 'Rietfontein' because it once had many reeds; ||xu-||kum-we is 'Modder River'; and !xabbu is 'Zout Rivier'.
summary.zh: 命名諸地者，螳螂也：|希霍亞即「蘆葦泉」，因昔多葦；巫烏巫庫姆威即「泥河」；！阿布即「鹽河」。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San place-lore from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The Bushmen say, it was the Mantis who once called the places names. |hii/hoa is 'Rietfontein', because it once had many reeds, while ||xu-||kum-we is 'Modder River'; that name is what white men call it. It was the Mantis who said: '|hii/hoa' and he also said ||xu-||kum-we. Then he said: '!xabbu' to 'Zout Rivier'.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), p. 67 (public domain).
